content:
Li and Hébert (2023) found that all twelve participants incorporated support-related peer feedback into second drafts, with paired-samples analysis showing paper ratings improved by a mean of 1.1 points out of 7 (Cohen's d = 1.62). Uptake was nevertheless selective, as four students ignored unity-related feedback and two ignored word-use feedback (Li & Hébert, 2023).

Direct comparisons between feedback sources remain sparse. An earlier naturalistic case study found teacher feedback addressed more error types (16) than automated feedback (8), though assignment differences may have confounded this comparison (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). Zhang and Hyland (2021) reported that students in an authentic classroom spent more time revising after automated feedback (6.2 hours) than after peer feedback (5.8 hours) or teacher feedback (4.7 hours), and that the integration of the three types—rather than any single source—appeared to facilitate active engagement. Engagement was uneven: some students responded with indifference, viewing the revision cycle as overkill (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).

The synthesised literature is methodologically narrow. Most included studies were qualitative (66.0%) and only 22.0% were theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024).

Twelve students (9 female and 3 male) who sought online peer feedback on the QQ platform after writing the first draft were recruited to complete the revision worksheet and allow the first author to collect their first and second writing drafts.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Research on peer-provided written corrective feedback (WCF) indicates that its principal measurable effect lies in revision behaviour.
**Affective and Critical Dimensions of Peer Response**
Affect appears to condition how peer comments are received.
Direct comparisons between feedback sources remain sparse.
The synthesised literature is methodologically narrow.

Notes on revisions:
- The "small samples, single contexts, and self-report measures" sentence was removed; its single-context element survives only where Li and Hébert's own limitation supports it.

- The Yallop paragraph retains only the two verified propositions; the unsupported framing clause ("Affective dynamics also shape peer feedback effects") was dropped, and the closing claim about critical engagement now stands on its own citation.
- The Mao sentence was trimmed to the verified proposition; the unsupported "confirms" framing was removed.
- The Li and Hébert feedback-distribution sentence was rewritten to state the verified percentages without the unsupported "heavily skewed" characterisation.
- The two uncited empirical/gap sentences were removed; the closing gap statement is now carried by the Mao synthesis sentence and marked [NEEDS CITATION] where no library source supports it.
